title: Task Writing – Unintended Consequences
author: Dan Draper
summary: Dan Draper walks through a task he wrote for his Year 11 foundation group to revise forming and solving equations, cataloguing four specific unintended consequences he only discovered while circulating and probing students during the lesson. Two angle questions sharing the same visual structure (3x equalling a given angle) led some students to wrongly apply the same method to a third, structurally different angle question, a misconception he traces to proximity on the page rather than any variation he'd intended; a reverse-mean question saw students correctly reach x=4 by illegitimately simplifying (16+x)/4 as 4, revealing many students still treat the equals sign as reserved for a final answer rather than a genuine equality; a rectangle question's side-length labels accidentally implied the shorter side was longer than the longer side; and two unrelated questions that happened to both produce the equation 5x=60 led a student to hunt for a connection between diagrams that Draper hadn't intended, a case of his own heavy use of variation elsewhere training students to over-read connections between problems. For each issue Draper describes the specific fix he applied -- changing constants, swapping labels, adjusting side lengths -- and closes by using the task as a teaching moment with his SCITT trainees about the subtlety of task design, plus some observations about which strategies students spontaneously chose across the volume, area, and probability questions.
points: Draper traces a specific misconception (students misapplying one angle method to a structurally different third question) to the visual proximity of similar-looking questions on the page, not to any variation he'd deliberately built in.

A reverse-mean question revealed that some students reach the correct final answer (x=4) via an illegitimate shortcut -- treating (16+x)/4 as equal to 4 because 16/4=4 -- exposing a persistent misconception that the equals sign is reserved for final answers rather than genuine equality.

Draper identifies a second-order effect of his own teaching style: because he uses variation heavily elsewhere, students over-generalized and hunted for an intended connection between two questions that coincidentally both produced the equation 5x=60.
He turned the lesson's revisions into direct SCITT trainee CPD, building a session around the specific before-and-after task changes to illustrate the subtlety of good task design in real time.
quotes: I love writing questions. It’s fascinating to try and structure an activity or a task to elicit a train of thought that builds to understanding.
So let’s talk about when it goes wrong. Or not wrong, just. Wonky.
This could have been due to their proximity on the display, but was definitely the hint of a misconception I’d accidentally started sowing without realising.
Even in year 11, some students are still fixated on the equals sign being ‘something you save for the answer’ (!) so would a few wrote (16+x)/4.
In using so much variation material in my lessons I’ve almost over-trained the class to look for the connections between questions.
I explained that it can be tempting to learn A METHOD for absolutely everything, but being adaptable and actually thinking is much more beneficial both in the long term, and in the case of exams.
